content.title: About
content.content: Halibut (Hippoglossus) is a large flatfish of the family Pleuronectidae, found in the cold northern waters of the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans. It has firm, white, mildly sweet flesh, low fat content, and a distinctive flattened body. Halibut is prized in cuisine for baking, grilling, poaching, and sushi.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Halibut can grow over 2.5 m in length and weigh more than 300 kg.
It is one of the most valuable commercial fish species, valued for its delicate flavor and texture.
Halibut changes sex during its life: younger individuals are males, older ones become females.
In the wild, halibut can live up to 50 years.
Its flesh contains lower mercury levels compared with many other large marine fish.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Halibut provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Compared with many fish, halibut has a low fat content, making it suitable for calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: Source of omega‑3
items.content: Despite its low fat, halibut still supplies beneficial omega‑3 fatty acids that support heart health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: It is rich in B12, B6, and niacin, which are important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Halibut contains selenium, phosphorus, and potassium, nutrients important for immunity, bone health, and blood pressure regulation.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to fish, including halibut.

items.title: Heavy‑metal contamination
items.content: Although mercury levels are generally low, choose fish from reputable sources, especially for children and pregnant women.

items.title: Possible parasites
items.content: Raw or undercooked fish can harbor parasites; proper cooking eliminates this risk.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Halibut is excellent baked in foil with lemon and herbs, pan‑seared, poached in broth, or used for sushi. The fillets can be cut into cubes for salads, soups, or stews.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Fresh halibut should be kept in the refrigerator at 0‑2 °C and used within 2 days. For longer storage, freeze it in an airtight bag at –18 °C; thaw in the refrigerator before use.
